primaries.primaryEn: The book opens with a disciple's humble question. In simple words: O Master, please teach me that most secret practice which protects people in every way — the one you have never told anyone until today. (Verse 1, Hindi.) This single prayer opens the entire Kavaca (armour) teaching that follows.

Brahmā answers: O learned one, there is indeed a most secret and holy armour of the Goddess that helps all beings — listen to it, O great sage. (Verse 2.) Combined with the commentary: whatever you asked for, O Brāhmaṇa, such a holy armour of the Goddess alone exists — keep it like a buried treasure. 'Great sage' is used because this teaching works for the welfare of all creatures.

Brahmā said: the armour that helps all beings, most secret and holy, is the Goddess's Kavaca itself — listen, O great sage. (Verse 2, Hindi.) In simple words the teacher confirms: yes, such a protective shield exists, it belongs to the Goddess alone, and hearing it with respect is itself a blessing.

First (Her name is) Śailaputrī, second Brahmacāriṇī, third Candraghaṇṭā, and fourth Kūṣmāṇḍā. (Verse 3.) Combined with the commentaries: because the Goddess is to be meditated as nine-formed, Her nine names are listed — and once you know a name, you easily recognise whom it points to. Śailaputrī: though supreme over all, out of love She accepted becoming the lowly mountain-king's daughter when He prayed with hard penance — what words can describe such love for devotees! Brahmacāriṇī: She whose nature is to carry seekers to Brahman, the blissful reality — giver of Brahmanhood. Candraghaṇṭā: She whose hand-bell shines spotless like the moon — the Goddess who makes hearts bloom with joy, more lovely even than the moon.

The first form is named Śailaputrī, the second Brahmacāriṇī, the third Candraghaṇṭā and the fourth Kuṣmāṇḍā. (Verse 3, Hindi.) In simple words the devotee counts the Mother's first four of nine forms on the fingers: the mountain's daughter, the maiden of Brahman, the moon-belled one, and the cosmic-egg warmer.

Fifth is called Skandamātā, sixth Kātyāyanī, seventh Kālarātrī, and eighth Mahāgaurī. (Verse 4.) Combined with the commentaries: Skandamātā — mother of Skanda (the scriptures say even wise men long to be born from such a womb, so pure is She). Kātyāyanī — She who appeared in sage Kātyāyana's hermitage for the gods' mission and was accepted as his daughter; ever-maiden, under no husband, fully free. Kālarātrī — the night that swallows even Time, the killer of all, since at the world's end even Time itself dies. Mahāgaurī — the greatly self-respecting one who, when called 'dark' by Śiva in jest, won a fair golden color by penance, as the Kālī Purāṇa tells clearly.

The ninth is famed as the giver of occult powers (Siddhidā) — thus the Nine Durgās are declared; and these names were spoken by the great-souled Brahmā himself. (Verse 5.) Combined with the commentary: 'giver of powers' means giver of final freedom; these nine are not nine different goddesses but nine faces of the one Durgā, like a yogi's many body-forms — and I (Brahmā) have declared exactly those forms the scriptures ask us to meditate.

That is why the armour is spoken of in the singular — 'the Kavaca of the Goddess'. And lest anyone doubt these names are man-made, the verse adds: the all-knowing great-souled Brahmā — the Veda itself — spoke all these names. (Verse 5, explanation.) Combined with the notes: one book reads 'Siddhidātrī' here; the Hindi prayer repeats — the ninth face is Siddhidātrī, these are the Nine Durgās, and every name comes from all-knowing Brahmā, the Veda-Lord Himself.

One burning in fire, fallen among enemies in battle, or terrified in rough and impassable places, if they take shelter (of Her) — (verses 6–7 begin). In simple words: whoever runs to the Mother while burning, trapped among enemies in war, or trembling in a dangerous lonely spot — listen to what happens to them next.

No evil befalls them even in the crisis of battle; I see for them no danger, no grief, no sorrow, no fear. (Verses 6–7.) Combined with the commentaries: whoever chants the nine names (supply this while reading), and even the many others who merely shelter behind that one chanter — for all of them, and for him, all harm is removed. That is the joint meaning of both verses: those burning, those war-trapped, those terror-struck in dreadful places — once sheltered, no mishap in battle, and as for sorrow, pain and fear, the seer declares: I simply do not see any for them.

Even by mere remembrance without deep devotion, the fear born of such dangers simply does not arise — so the verse declares. (Explanation of verse 7.) In simple words: you don't even need perfect devotion; just remembering Her once is enough to keep fear away.

Whoever is burning in fire, fallen among enemies in battle, or terrified in rough impassable places and reaches the shelter of Goddess Durgā — no evil touches them even in war's crisis. I see no calamity of any kind for such a person — no grief, no sorrow, no fear. (Verses 6–7, Hindi.) In simple words the devotee repeats the promise slowly: fire, enemies, wilderness — take shelter once, and no harm, no sorrow, no fear can touch you.

But by those by whom (She) is remembered with devotion — theirs, surely, is prosperity. (Then) Cāmuṇḍā seated on a corpse, Vārāhī riding a buffalo. (Verse 8.) In simple words: the frightened get protection (verses 6–7); but those who remember Her with love get more — certain growth and glory. Then the hymn begins describing the Seven Mothers who guard the chanter.

Aindrī mounted on an elephant, Vaiṣṇavī seated on Garuḍa; Māheśvarī riding a bull, Kaumārī with the peacock as vehicle. (Verse 9.) In simple words: Indra's power rides the elephant, Viṣṇu's power rides Garuḍa, Śiva's power rides the bull, Kumāra's power rides the peacock — the Mother's seven warrior faces, each on Her own mount.

Having told the fruit of devotion in distress, now the fruit of the seeker's devotion: 'by whomsoever' — theirs is attainment. One reading says 'perfection' (siddhi) instead of 'prosperity' — and perfection means true knowledge. Then, ever-active for removing devotees' troubles, come the Seven Mothers, described across two verses (8–9). Combined with the notes: remembrance with love surely brings the earlier fruit — and what to say of it, it brings the four goals of life (duty, wealth, desire, freedom) too. One book reads 'growth' (vṛddhi) for 'prosperity'. The Goddess's overflowing motherly love is shown here only to grow our devotion.

The mount of the Goddess is Garuḍa (Vaiṣṇavī); Māheśvarī rides the bull; Kaumārī's vehicle is the peacock. (Verses 8–9, Hindi.) In simple words the devotee pictures each Mother on Her own mount — corpse, buffalo, elephant, Garuḍa, bull, peacock — seven guardians shining together.

A caution about extra verses: after 'remembered with devotion' some books add 'those who remember You, O Lord of gods, You protect them, no doubt' — but ancient explainers like Nīlakaṇṭha and Bhāskararāya never accepted it in the Kavaca. Likewise after verse 9 some copies carry three verses on Lakṣmī, the white-formed Goddess, Nārasiṃhī and Śivadūtī — also unexplained by old commentators, so left out. And before verse 10's second half some read 'all these Mothers, rich in all yogas' — also not accepted by the ancients. (For detail the edition points to Paṇḍit Rājakiśoramaṇi Tripathī's Devī-Māhātmya study.) In simple words: only the verses the old masters explain belong to the real Kavaca; later additions, however sweet, are kept out.

Brāhmī seated on a swan, adorned with every ornament; shining with many jewels and many decorations. (Verse 10.) In simple words: Brahmā's power glides on a swan, dressed in all ornaments — the first of the Mothers in their full glory.

Goddesses are seen mounted on chariots, blazing with anger — conch, discus, mace, spear, plough and club as weapons. (Verse 11.) In simple words: beyond the seven, more warrior goddesses roll in on chariots, furious to protect, holding conch and discus and mace.

Shield and javelin too, axe and noose; the spear-weapon and the trident, and the supreme wonderful bow. (Verse 12.) In simple words the armoury list continues — shield, spear, axe, noose, lance, trident and the finest of bows — heaven's whole arsenal in the Mothers' hands.

To destroy the demons' bodies, to grant fearlessness to devotees, and for the welfare of the gods — thus they hold these weapons. (Verse 13.) Combined with the commentaries: other goddesses beyond the seven, also mounted on chariots in anger for devotees' protection, are seen — by gods and men. Their weapons are then listed (verses 10–12). And why do the Seven Mothers hold conch, discus and the rest? For three reasons together: to finish demons' bodies, to give devotees fearlessness, and to serve the gods. The feeling behind it: even unasked, these great goddesses rush to protect the world purely out of motherly love — so why should unlucky little me not beg them for my own protection, like a child asking its mother?

O mighty, O greatly eager, O destroyer of great fear — protect me, O Goddess hard to behold, O increaser of the foes' terror! (Verse 14.) Combined with the commentaries: from here the devotee himself starts praying. Read this prayer-mantra first, then the Kavaca — that is the rule. 'Great strength' is Her power of illusion itself; 'great eagerness' is Her zeal to protect the world; 'destroyer of great fear' destroys death-like terror by giving wisdom; 'hard to behold' — Her form stands beyond sight, as the scripture says; and the 'foes' are lust, anger and their kin.

O greatly strong! O greatly eager! O destroyer of great fears! O hard to behold! O increaser of the foes' terror! O Goddess, protect me. (Verse 14, Hindi.) In simple words the devotee cries out Her titles one by one — strength, zeal, fear-killer, unseeable, terror to enemies — and begs: protect me.

In the east may Aindrī protect me; in the south-east the fire-goddess. In the south, protect, O Vārāhī; in the south-west, O sword-bearer. (Verse 15.) Combined with the commentaries: grammar first — where the goddess-name ends in the nominative ('may Aindrī protect'), the verb runs in third person; where it ends in address ('protect, O Vārāhī'), it runs in second person — each verb simply carries forward to its own line. Meaning: Aindrī, Indra's power standing in the east, protect me (or: protect me standing in the east — both read the same, since power and its holder are one). Vārāhī is Yama's power (Varāha = Yama in ancient usage) — O Vārāhī, standing in the south, protect me. The sword-bearer is Nirṛti's power in the south-west. One book reads 'hard to behold' (duṣprekṣye) in verse 14.

In the west may Vāruṇī protect; in the north-west, She who rides a deer. In the north may Kaumārī protect; in the north-east, She who holds a spear. (Verse 16.) Combined with the commentary: the deer-rider is the wind-god's power (the wind rides a deer); Kaumārī here is Kubera's power (Kumāra = Kubera, whose pride is ugly — the joke hidden in the name), guarding the north though her full station comes later — and one goddess guarding two stations is no fault at all; or She is the Kaumārī among the Seven Mothers, and the spear-holder is Īśāna's power.

The Hindi of the same prayer: the deer-rider's openly stated station comes ahead, yet one goddess guarding two stations is no contradiction — whether as Kubera's power or as the Kaumārī of the Seven Mothers, and the spear-holder as Īśāna's power. (Verse 16, explanation.) In simple words: don't worry if one Mother guards two directions — a mother can watch two children at once.

In the west may Vāruṇī, in the north-west the deer-riding Goddess protect me. In the north Kaumārī and in the north-east the spear-holding Goddess protect me. (Verse 16, Hindi.) In simple words the devotee turns around the compass — west, north-west, north, north-east — posting a Mother at every corner.

Above may Brāhmī protect me, and below likewise Vaiṣṇavī. Thus in all ten directions may Cāmuṇḍā, who rides a corpse, protect. (Verse 17.) Combined with the commentary: 'O Brāhmī' — You who bring Brahmā (fetch and revive all beings), standing above, protect me (or: protect my upper part — same sense). So too below. Then 'thus' — in the manner of the ten direction-guardians — may Cāmuṇḍā protect my ten directions, my kin-directions; for Cāmuṇḍā stationed in all ten directions protects me — that is the settled meaning, since merely guarding empty directions would serve no purpose.

O Brāhmī, protect me in the upper region, and may Vaiṣṇavī protect me below. Likewise may Cāmuṇḍā, who makes a corpse Her vehicle, protect me in all ten directions. (Verse 17, Hindi.) In simple words: sky above, earth below, and all ten sides around — every direction gets its guarding Mother, with corpse-riding Cāmuṇḍā watching the whole circle.

May Jayā stand before me, Vijayā behind; Ajitā to my left, and Aparājitā to my right. (Verse 18.) Combined with the commentaries: 'let her stand' in the ancient style; Jayā is a power-goddess — may she stand firm, all for my protection.

May Udyotinī guard (my) hair-top, Umā stationed on the crown; Mālādhārī on the forehead, and Yaśasvinī guard the brows. (Verse 19.) Combined with the commentaries: read every limb the same way — the goddess named Udyotinī, stationed at my hair-top, guards my hair-top; and so for each. Wherever the verse names only the station (first line) supply 'guarding', and wherever only guarding (second line) supply 'stationed' — apply this joining rule everywhere through the whole body-list.

Whatever of the two patterns is unsaid in either place, supply the other one there. (Explanation of the joining rule, verse 19.) In simple words the commentators give the key to the whole list: each line either says where She stands or what She guards — you silently add the missing half, and the meaning completes itself, everywhere alike.

Trinetrā between the brows, and Yamaghaṇṭā at the nose; Śaṅkhinī between the eyes, Dvāravāsinī at the ears. (Verse 20.) In simple words the guard-posting moves down the face: the three-eyed one between the brows, the death-bell at the nose, the conch-lady between the eyes, the door-keeper at the ears.

May Kālikā guard the cheeks, Śaṅkarī the ear-roots; Sugandhā the nose, and Carcikā the upper lip. (Verse 21.) In simple words: Kālī on the cheeks, Śaṅkarī at the ear-roots, sweet-fragrance goddess on the nose, Carcikā on the upper lip — every feature covered.

Amṛtakalā on the lower lip, Sarasvatī on the tongue; may Kaumārī guard the teeth, and Caṇḍikā the throat's middle. (Verse 22.) Combined with the variant note: some books read 'protect' (pātu) for 'guard', 'throat-region' for 'throat-middle', and 'Śāṅkarī' for 'Śaṅkarī' — small music-changes in the same prayer.

Citra-ghaṇṭā at the throat-bell, Mahāmāyā at the palate; may Kāmākṣī guard the chin, and Sarvamaṅgalā my speech. (Verse 23.) Combined with the commentaries: 'at the nostrils' means at the nose-holes (while later 'nose' alone means the nose-bridge); 'lower' means the lower lip. The Hindi prayer repeats verses 20–23 limb by limb: three-eyed one at brow-centre guards brows; death-bell at nose guards nostrils; conch-lady in both eyes guards eyes; door-keeper in both ears guards ears (20); Kālikā on cheeks, Śaṅkarī at ear-roots, Sugandhā on nose, Carcikā on upper lip guard each in turn (21); nectar-digit on lower lip, Sarasvatī on tongue, Kaumārī on teeth, Caṇḍikā mid-throat guard each (22); bell-pictured goddess at throat-bell, Great Illusion at palate, love-eyed goddess at chin, all-blessing goddess on speech guard each (23).

Bhadrakālī at the neck, Dhanurdharī on the spine; Nīlagrīvā outside the throat, Nalakūbarī at the windpipe. (Verse 24.) In simple words the guard moves to neck and back: kindly-Kālī on the neck, bow-bearer on the spine, blue-throated one on the throat's outside, Kubera's lady at the windpipe.

May sword-bearer guard both shoulders, Vajradhāriṇī my arms; may Daṇḍinī guard the hands, and Ambikā the fingers. (Verse 25.) Combined with the commentaries: 'windpipe' means the throat-tube; the throat's outer part is the outer throat. 'Arm' means shoulder-to-elbow, 'hand' means elbow-to-fingertips — so each goddess knows exactly her stretch. The Hindi prayer repeats: Bhadrakālī guards the neck, bow-bearer the spine, blue-throated the outer throat, Nalakūbarī the windpipe (24); sword-bearer both shoulders, thunderbolt-bearer both my arms (25, continued next).

Daṇḍinī stationed in both hands guards both hands, and Ambikā stationed in the fingers guards the fingers. (Verse 25, Hindi, with variant note.) Combined with the variant: some books read 'may the sword-lady guard the shoulders' — same guard, slightly different music.

May Śūleśvarī guard the nails, Naleśvarī the belly; Mahādevī the breasts, and Śokavināśinī the mind. (Verse 26.) In simple words: spear-lady on the nails, belly-goddess on the belly, Great Goddess on the breasts, grief-destroyer on the mind.

Lalitā the heart, Śūladhāriṇī the belly; Kāminī the navel, and Guhyeśvarī the secret part. (Verse 27.) In simple words: the lovely one guards the heart, the spear-holder the stomach, the loving one the navel, the secret-lady the secret place.

Bhūtanāthā the generative organ, Mahiṣavāhinī the anus; Bhagavatī the waist, Vindhyavāsinī the knees. (Verse 28, with the next verse quoted.) Combined with the old note: 'Mahābalā is declared at the shanks, Vināyakī between the knees, Nārasiṃhī at the ankles, Amitaujasī on the foot-top' (verse 29) — the guard-list marches down the legs.

Śrīdharī the toes, Talavāsinī dwelling under the feet; Karālī the toenails and teeth, and Ūrdhvakeśinī the hair. (Verse 30, with verse 31 quoted.) Combined with the commentaries: 'dweller at the foot' is one phrase, 'under-dweller' means underworld-dweller; 'under the feet' and 'underworld-dwelling' are separate words. Then verse 31: Kauberī in the hair-pores, Vāgīśvarī on the skin — and Pārvatī in blood, marrow, fat, flesh, bone and medulla. Guptavatī adds: Mahābalā is 'declared' — famous from the ancient lore-books — as the epithet of the great-strong Goddess. Pradīpa adds the old approved readings and the comforting rule: just as one goddess guarding two stations is no fault, two goddesses guarding one station is equally fine — which is why both toenails and teeth get Karālī.

The reasoning why one station may hold two guards and one guard two stations — so Karālī guards both toenails and teeth without contradiction. (Explanation of verses 30–31.) In simple words the commentators settle the doubt: sharing guard-duty, in either direction, breaks no rule — a mother can watch two children, and two mothers can watch one child.

Kauberī in the hair-pores guards the pores, Vāgīśvarī on the skin guards the skin; Pārvatī dwelling in blood, marrow, fat, flesh, bone and medulla guards them all. (Verse 31, Hindi, with variants.) Combined with the variant list: some books read Kuleśvarī, 'in the heart', 'in the belly', 'at the navel', 'Pūtanā-Kāmikā for the organ', 'at the anus', 'giver of all desired boons', 'bright ones on the foot-top', 'may Śrī guard the toes', 'Karālī of nails and fangs'. Then the Hindi prayer of verses 28–31: Bhūtanāthā, buffalo-rider, Bhagavatī and Vindhya-dweller guard organ, anus, waist and both knees (28); declared Mahābalā the shanks, Vināyakī between knees, Nārasiṃhī the ankles, mighty Amitaujasī the foot-top (29); Śrīdharī the toes, under-feet-dweller the soles, Karālī the toenails and teeth, sky-haired one the hair (30); pore-dweller Kauberī the pores, speech-lady Vāgīśvarī the skin (31, continued).

Kālarātri the entrails, Mukuṭeśvarī the bile; Padmāvatī in the lotus-cave, and Cūḍāmaṇi in phlegm. (Verse 32.) Combined with the commentaries: 'in the lotus-cave' — the lotus is the heart and such; the goddess stationed in the breath dwelling there guards that breath, say some. Others say, since breath-guarding comes later, 'lotus-cave' here means the heart itself, as the scripture calls the heart 'like a lotus-cave, facing down'. Cūḍāmaṇi is the goddess famed in the Raktāsura-killing.

The heart itself, called 'lotus-cave facing down' by scripture, is what the name means here — and Cūḍāmaṇi is famed from the Raktāsura battle. (Verse 32, explanation.) In simple words the debate is settled gently: whether breath or heart, the Mother's guard covers the chest's innermost core.

Kālarātri dwelling in the entrails guards them; Mukuṭeśvarī in bile guards bile; Padmāvatī in the lotus-cave guards it; Cūḍāmaṇi in phlegm guards phlegm. (Verse 32, Hindi.) In simple words the inner organs get their guards too — entrails, bile, heart-cave, phlegm — nothing inside left unwatched.

Jvālāmukhī at the nail-flames, Abhedyā in all the joints; may Brāhmī guard my semen, and Chatreśvarī my shadow. (Verse 33.) In simple words: flame-faced goddess on the nails' glow, unbreakable goddess in every joint, Brahmā's power on vitality, umbrella-lady on the shadow.

Ego, mind and intellect guard for me, O follower of righteousness — and the five breaths: prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, samāna, udāna. (Verse 34, with variant.) Combined with the variant: some books read 'O holder of righteousness' (dharmadhāriṇī) for 'O follower of righteousness'.

Fame, glory and fortune — may Cakriṇī always guard; O Indrāṇī, guard my family-line; O Caṇḍikā, guard my cattle. (Verse 35.) Combined with the commentaries: here 'mind' means the whole inner mind-stuff (so the mind has four parts with the heart — no repetition with verse 26's grief-destroyer; or read it as 'She who destroys the mind's grief'). The five breaths are named in one breath as a group. Pradīpa adds: 'nail-flame' is the glow living in nails; the Unbreakable goddess stationed in all joints guards all joints; 'O Brāhmī, guard my vitality.' On verse 34's address the word 'you' is silently supplied, and the command runs in second person; on 35 too. The Hindi prayer continues: flame-faced on nail-glow, Unbreakable in all joints, Brāhmī on vitality, umbrella-lady on shadow (33); follower-of-righteousness on ego, mind, intellect and all five breaths (34). Then a caution: some copies add two extra verses here (thunderbolt-handed guarding breath; Yoginī in taste-form-smell-sound-touch; Nārāyaṇī guarding goodness-passion-darkness; Vārāhī guarding life, Vaiṣṇavī guarding duty) — but the ancients never took them, so they stay out of the original.

May Mahālakṣmī guard sons, Bhairavī the wife; Kṣemakarī the road, Vijayā dwelling everywhere. (Verse 36, with variants.) Combined with the variants: some read 'wealth and learning' for 'sons'; and some carry a longer road-verse — 'guard the path well, guard the road with welfare; Mahālakṣmī at the king's door, Vijayā dwelling everywhere'.

Whatever station lacks guard, left out of the armour — all that guard for me, O Goddess, O Jayantī, destroyer of sins. (Verse 37, with verse 38 quoted.) Combined with the old note: 'if he wishes his own good, let him not take one step without the armour' — always wrapped in the Kavaca, wherever he goes. In simple words the devotee adds a safety net: Mother, any spot this long list may have missed — cover that too, O ever-victorious sin-destroyer.

There and there is gain of aims, and victory fulfilling all desires; whatever wish he thinks of, that he surely obtains. (Verse 39.) In simple words the fruit begins: wherever the armour-wearer goes, profit follows; victory that fulfils every wish follows; every thought-wish comes true — guaranteed.

Unmatched supreme lordship he shall win on earth; fearless becomes the mortal, undefeated in battles. (Verse 40.) In simple words: peerless power on this earth, zero fear, and no defeat in any fight — that is the Kavaca-wearer's fortune.

Worshipped in all three worlds becomes the man wrapped in the armour; and this armour of the Goddess is hard even for gods to get. (Verse 41.) Combined with the commentaries: verses 36–37 name the fruit of wearing; verse 38 ('not one step without it') means: without the worn armour — don't move an inch if you want your own good; never let a moment pass without the Goddess in mind. The old Purāṇa line is quoted: sleeping, standing, walking, talking, delighting in food — always chant the Goddess, and you are freed from bondage. So after teaching the rule, the hymn tells the fruit: wrapped, wherever he goes (38–41).

'Always chant the Goddess — sleeping, standing, walking, talking, delighting in food — and you are freed from bondage,' say the Purāṇas. So taught the rule, now the fruit is told. (Verse 38's seal.) In simple words: remembrance has no off-hours — chant moving, resting, eating — and every bondage breaks.

He becomes free of fear; worshipped in the three worlds, the armour-wrapped man; this armour of the Goddess is rare even for gods. (Verses 40–41, Hindi.) In simple words the devotee repeats the promise with joy: no fear, honoured in heaven-earth-underworld, holding something even gods can hardly get.

Whoever reads with discipline, daily, at all three twilights, full of faith — divine lustre comes to him, and in all three worlds he is undefeated. (Verse 42.) In simple words: dawn, noon, dusk — read with rule and faith every day, and you shine with goddess-glow, unbeaten anywhere.

He lives a hundred years and more, free of sudden death; all diseases perish — skin-blisters, smallpox and the rest. (Verse 43.) In simple words: full lifespan past a hundred, no accidents, and every illness — from rashes to poxes — wiped out.

Stationary poisons, moving poisons, and man-made poisons too; all black-magic rites on earth, all spells and diagrams. (Verse 44.) In simple words the protection-list widens: plant poisons, snake poisons, lab-made poisons, every evil rite and every magic circle on earth.

Earth-roamers and sky-roamers, water-born and teaching-born; inborn and family-born troops — Ḍākinī and Śākinī too. (Verse 45.) In simple words: every creepy host is named — crawlers, flyers, water-spirits, spell-learnt ones, inborn and clan-bound hordes, Ḍākinīs and Śākinīs.

Sky-roaming terrors, and hugely strong Ḍākinīs; planets, ghosts, goblins, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, demons. (Verse 46.) In simple words: sky-terrors, mighty witch-hosts, seizure-spirits, ghosts, goblins, nature-spirits, musicians of heaven, man-eaters — the whole roster.

Brahma-demons, vampires, Kūṣmāṇḍas, Bhairavas and the rest — perish at his very sight, once the armour rests in his heart. (Verse 47.) In simple words: the darkest ones — brahmin-ghosts, corpse-risers, imp hordes, fierce Bhairava troops — melt away just by looking at the man whose heart holds the Kavaca.

The king honours him more and more; it grows supreme brilliance; and he too grows with fame, garlanding the earth with glory. (Verse 48.) Combined with the commentaries: 'stationary' poison means aconite and such; 'moving' means snakes and the like; 'man-made' means mixed poisons like honey-and-ghee in equal measure gone wrong. 'Family-born' and the rest are classes of dark deities; 'teaching-born' are petty spirits perfected by mere instruction. 'Divine lustre' is the glow of pure consciousness. The Hindi prayer repeats verses 42–48 whole: thrice-daily faithful reading gives goddess-glow and three-world victory (42); hundred-plus years, no sudden death, all diseases dead (43); then every poison — plant, snake-scorpion, and mixed things like opium and oil blends — every spell, diagram and black rite on earth; crawlers, flyers, water-born, teaching-born, inborn, clan troops, garland-Ḍākinīs, Śākinīs, sky-terrors, mighty Ḍākinīs, planets, ghosts, goblins, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, demons, brahmin-ghosts, vampires, Kuṣmāṇḍas, Bhairavas — all perish merely at the sight of the armour-hearted man; and that best of men rises in royal honour, blazes with supreme glow, and grows in fame that garlands the earth (44–48).

Having first worn the armour, let him chant the Seven-hundred Cāṇḍī — as long as the earth-disc holds mountains, forests and woods. (Verse 49.) In simple words the rule of order: first wear the Kavaca, then chant the Saptashatī — and the fruit lasts as long as the earth itself stands with its mountains and forests.

So long shall his line of sons and grandsons stand on earth; after the body's end, the supreme station, hard even for gods. (Verse 50.) In simple words: your children and grandchildren stay rooted on earth as long as the world lasts — and after death, you reach the highest place, which even gods find hard to win.
That supreme station the man surely wins, always, by Mahāmāyā's grace. (Verse 51.) In simple words: not by effort alone — by the Great Mother Illusion's own grace, surely and forever.

Thus ends the holy armour of the Goddess. Combined with the two closers: the Kavaca must be worn first and then the Saptashatī chanted — that order itself proves the armour belongs to the Caṇḍī recitation as its limb; earlier the hymn spoke other side-fruits too, but by the law of side-desires those extra practices stand outside without fault. 'As long as the earth-disc' is praise-speech like 'full-perfection fruit-speech'. 'First' means first in time only — and since no gaplessness is taught here, the night-hymn wrap-around is explained elsewhere ('read the night-hymn first'); by Vedic order (beginning-middle-end words and the step-word), the night-hymn comes first and the nine-lettered mantra sits before it. So too the Argala's 'having read this hymn, let man read the great hymn' teaches only limb-and-whole kinship — as with 'having eaten today, he goes tomorrow', the -having-done form allows a gap, so the Vedic order stands unharmed and no gap breaks it. By the drawing-together rule (as with the ten-callers' calls and chants), the order is fixed: Kavaca, Argala, nine-lettered, night-hymn, Caṇḍī-praise; and after counting praise-and-chant come Goddess-hymn, nine-lettered and mysteries, in order. (Verses 49–51, Guptavatī's seal on the Kavaca explanation.)

Quoted scriptures confirm: 'whom the Self chooses, by him It is won' — and 'who knows this power of illusion conquers death, crosses sin, reaches deathlessness' — and 'I Myself speak this, tasted by gods and men' — and 'Pārvatī is the supreme wisdom, giver of Brahman-wisdom.' (Pradīpa's seal, verses 50–51.) In simple words the old books all agree: the Supreme chooses Its own; knowing the Mother's power means victory over death, sin and mortality itself.

Whoever first reads the armour and then reads the Saptashatī or Caṇḍī — his line of sons and grandsons stays on earth as long as the earth-disc holds mountains, forests and woods. And after the body's end, by holy Mahāmāyā's grace he surely reaches that eternal supreme station, hard even for gods. (Verses 49–51, Hindi.) One book adds 'he gains the supreme form and rejoices with Śiva' — but since most books don't agree, it stays out of the original. Then the Argala hymn begins: its seer is Viṣṇu, metre anuṣṭup, deity great Lakṣmī, purpose — pleasing Mother Jagadambā as a limb of the Saptashatī chant; and Mārkaṇḍeya speaks.

Jayantī, Maṅgalā, Kālī, Bhadrakālī, Kapālinī; Durgā, Kṣamā, Śivā, Dhātrī — Svāhā, Svadhā, salutation to You! (Argala verse 1.) Combined with the commentaries: the grammar joins possessive endings simply ('victorious one' and the rest); then the praise begins with the Goddess aimed at by meditation, listing Her qualities fit for focus. Jayantī: the topmost victor — the Mother as Brahman veiled by the three qualities, cause of all. Maṅgalā: She who takes away devotees' creeping through birth-and-death and grants freedom — 'his breaths do not depart' says scripture. Kālī: She who swallows all this at world-end — 'Brahman and warriorhood both become His food, with Death as sauce' says scripture. Bhadrakālī: She who takes goodness and joy to give devotees, 'giver of joy' as the secret lore says. Kapālinī: skull means head-bone (says the dictionary) — She who killed Brahmā and the rest and roams at world-end holding their skulls; or lotus-universe in hand; the secret lore hails Her 'lotus-universe-handed supreme Kapālinī'. Durgā: reached with pain through yoga, ritual and worship — 'that Durgā, hard to reach' says the Atharvaśiras. Kṣamā: She who bears all faults of devotees and others, being Mother, overflowing with mercy. Śivā: Herself pure consciousness — as the Sūta Saṃhitā sings at length: the changeless, ever-blissful awareness, destroyer of worldliness, supreme Goddess, one with Śiva, maker of good. Dhātrī: holder of the whole expanse — 'I move with Rudras and Vasus, I bear Mitra-Varuṇa, Indra-Agni and the Aśvins' says scripture. Svāhā feeds the gods, Svadhā feeds the ancestors. O possessor of all these great qualities — to You, salutation alone; for serving such a One in full, who has the strength? The Hindi prayer begins: Mārkaṇḍeya ṛṣi, teaching his students the Goddess's praise, said — Jayantī 1, Maṅgalā 2 … (continued).

The seer asks: what did He say? All this — know that the Saptashatī hymn itself, which by its stated method destroys the curse-like bolt blocking all mantra success, is the un-bolter (abhikīlaka); worship it as such. And if you ask whether other mantra practices give no safety, that they surely can't be abandoned for this alone — the answer comes: even the man constantly busy chanting this Saptashatī hymn, plus the man busy with many other mantras, both reach all welfare. (Verse 2, with Pradīpa.) Combined with the Hindi: the Saptashatī hymn that removes the curse-bolt blocking mantra success must be fully known; yet one absorbed in other mantras' chanting also reaches welfare.

By this (hymn) expulsion-rites and all things succeed for those who praise the Goddess — by the hymn alone She is won. (Verse 3.) Combined with the commentaries: the man devoted to chanting finds even expulsion-rites and all hard-to-get things succeeding; and to men who chant only mantras without Saptashatī-reading, success by mere mantra-chant was already granted — now, to men who read only the Saptashatī without mantra-chanting either, the hymn grants every success by mere reading of this famed hymn: the Goddess Herself, of true-being-consciousness-bliss form, is pleased. The Hindi repeats: besides Saptashatī-reading, other mantras' chanting also fulfils expulsion and all aims — but those who praise with this hymn alone win the Goddess of blissful reality Herself. (Continued next.)

Those who praise with this Saptashatī hymn alone win the blissful-reality Goddess Herself, by the hymn alone. (Verse 3, Hindi completion.) In simple words: other paths work, but this hymn by itself is enough to win Her — that is its special promise.

No mantra there, no herb, nothing else at all is found — without any chanting, all expulsion-rites and the rest succeed. (Verse 4.) Combined with the commentaries: someone may fear — if the easy Caṇḍī-praise makes all hard-won lores useless, why keep them? The verse answers: for that man's success no other mantra is of use, no herb, no yoga-power or other means at all — yet without any mantra-chanting ritual, all expulsion rites and every wished-for work succeed by the hymn alone. So far: by Saptashatī-practice alone all welfare comes; and by other-mantra practice too all welfare comes — both paths are proved true. The Hindi repeats: readers of Saptashatī need no mantra, no herb, no other means — without chanting-rituals, all expulsion and all aims succeed by reading alone. (Continued next.)

Without chanting-rituals their expulsion-rites and all aims succeed — by reading alone. (Verse 4, Hindi completion.) In simple words: no herbs, no extra mantras, no instruments — just read, and everything succeeds.

To remove people's doubt about all the lores, Hara invited them — 'all this is wholly good.' (Verse 5.) Combined with Guptavatī: He invited — He thought it over and showed His thinking. 'All' means: once this bolt-making is done, the whole family of lores becomes good and fruitful — people fulfilled by mere Caṇḍī-praise alone may drop all other duty-wealth-desire-freedom scriptures without loss. So the bolt was built by Śiva to block praise-born successes, in order to keep the other lores meaningful — that is the sense of all four verses (2–5).

The bolt was built by Śiva to block successes born of mere praise, so that the other lores keep their purpose — that is the sense of verses 2–5. (Explanation.) In simple words: the lock exists to protect the value of every other sacred science; without it, one easy hymn would empty all other paths.

The people's two-sided doubt — 'both these paths exist, but which?' — Hara first removed by inviting them, as if to say: come, I shall clear this doubt. (Pradīpa on verse 5.) Combined with the Hindi: 'Can everything really succeed by Saptashatī alone, with no other chanting?' — holding this doubt of people's minds before Him, Lord Śiva thought it over and decided: this Saptashatī-hymn reading alone is best and most blesse.

Lord Śiva invited all, thought it over, and decided: reading this Saptashatī hymn alone is supreme and blessing-giving. (Verse 5, Hindi completion.) In simple words the doubt is settled from God's own mouth: this hymn alone is enough — and best.

But His hymn of Caṇḍikā — that He made secret; and of the merit there is no ending — know that restraint exactly as it is. (Verse 6.) Combined with the commentaries: then He made this very Saptashatī hymn of Caṇḍikā top-secret — making the second path (praise alone) the essence, over the first path (mantra-chanting). So Mārkaṇḍeya told the old tale from the Tantras; then, teaching disciples the Saptashatī's glory, he tells Śiva's intent: the fruit born of reading this hymn never ends, ever — while mantra-chanting-born merit does end. So know exactly as it is that restraint (niyantraṇā) which Śiva built — the narrowing of the first path. One book reads 'they succeed' (sidhyanti) here. The Hindi repeats: Mahādeva made this Saptashatī hymn of Caṇḍikā secret — because other mantras' chant-born merit fades with time, while Saptashatī-reading-born merit never fades. (Continued next.)
So know as exact truth Śiva's decision preferring Saptashatī over all other mantras. (Verse 6, Hindi completion.) In simple words: God Himself ranked this hymn first — believe it exactly as told.

He too attains all welfare, no doubt — on the dark fourteenth or the eighth, composed. (Verse 7.) Combined with Guptavatī: don't think the hymn's power is lost altogether by the lock. To one who learns the unbolting method from the guru's mouth and practises exactly so, success comes as before, needing no other lore at all — then He shows that very method: 'on the dark (fourteenth)' means in whichever month fresh earnings come, in that month — supply the rest. (Continued in Pradīpa.)

The unbolting method is then shown: on the dark fourteenth or eighth of the month of fresh earnings. (Verse 7, Guptavatī completion.) In simple words: the lock has a key — learn it from the teacher, use it on the dark 14th or 8th, and the old full power returns.

Even the other-mantra chanter, if he joins this hymn's chanting, attains all welfare — so everyone should honour Saptashatī-reading above all. This also teaches: other mantras must be chanted only after reading Saptashatī, or their fruit won't come — because this hymn alone destroys whatever blocks all mantra success, which is why it was first called the un-bolter. 'Un-bolter' means the fault-form that dams success; destroying it, the hymn earns the same name by pointer-sense. And if you ask — doesn't this hymn also need nine-lettered-mantra chanting? — we say: that is only for quicker fruit, not that without it this hymn bears none; whereas without this hymn, those mantras bear none at all — that is the special point. (Verse 7, Pradīpa.)

That (mantra-chanter) too attains welfare, no doubt — the meditator, on the dark fourteenth or eighth. (Verse 7, Hindi.) In simple words: join this hymn to any other chanting and welfare is certain — and mark the dark 14th or 8th for the special rite (told in the next verse).

He gives and he receives back — not otherwise is She pleased. In this form, by the bolt, Mahādeva bolted (it). (Verse 8.) Combined with the commentaries: 'gives and receives' — by two verbs joined, one single rite named give-and-take is ordained; its exact form the Guru-kīlaka chapter will open up. But, disciples — knowing this hymn grants unthinkable fruit to all, and all would become all-powerful, Mahādeva bolted it. On the dark 14th or 8th, composed, the worshipper offers all his rightly-earned wealth to the Goddess — 'O Goddess, from now all this wealth of mine is given by me to You' — then, to run his worldly life, he takes it back as Her grace-gift ('take this wealth as My grace'), spends it by righteous-law paths, and stays ever Hers; to him alone the Saptashatī is pleased — not otherwise. By such a success-damming bolt Mahādeva bolted it; and this bolt's secret the mystery-lore's Guru-bolt chapter shows — we shall open it ahead. (Continued in Hindi next.)

By such a success-damming bolt Mahādeva bolted it — a secret the lore's Guru-bolt chapter shows, to be opened ahead. (Verse 8, Pradīpa completion.) Combined with the Hindi prayer: whoever offers his all in the Goddess's service — surrenders everything — and then takes it back as grace-food, on him alone She is pleased; without this, Her pleasure is not won. By such a bolt Mahādeva keeps this Saptashatī hymn bolted. (Verse 8.)

Whoever, having unbolted Her, chants Her daily, clearly — he becomes perfected, he becomes Her troop, and a Gandharva is born on earth. (Verse 9.) In simple words: unbolt Her by the give-and-take rite above, chant daily with clear voice — and you become a perfected one, join Her own hosts, and walk the earth as a Gandharva, heaven's singer-guardian.

And roaming everywhere, no fear is born for him anywhere; nor does he fall to sudden death — dead, he wins freedom. (Verse 10.) In simple words: wander the whole world with zero fear anywhere; no accident can take him; and at death — liberation itself.

Having known, he should begin and do — not doing, he is destroyed. So the wise begin it only after knowing it fully. (Verse 11.) Combined with the notes: 'begins and does' means begins and renounces (the doubt); not renouncing, he is destroyed — left without success. One book reads 'he succeeds' for 'he begins', and 'a man is born' elsewhere. In simple words: learn the unbolting first, then start — starting blind ruins the work; so the wise master it first, then begin.

Whatever fortune and the rest is seen in womankind — all of it by Her grace; so this blessed hymn must be chanted after unbolting. (Verse 12.) Combined with the commentaries: 'knowing, he should do' is the act of giving up doubt after knowledge begins; giving it up, he is destroyed — success-less. So, because it stands thus, the wise begin this hymn only after knowing the bolt — fully equipped and fault-free. The talk of ruin serves only to show the bolt-knowledge is a must — since casual reading too is allowed by other sayings. 'By Her grace' means for that reason. One book reads 'he succeeds' and 'a man is born'. The Hindi prayer continues: whoever unbolts this hymn as told and chants daily with clear voice becomes perfected — joins Her hosts — and becomes the all-world-guarding Gandharva, singer of Her glories (9); roaming everywhere yet fearing nowhere, never seized by sudden death, and freed after death (10); so learn this unbolting process, remove it, and only then begin the Saptashatī — skipping it leaves wishes unfulfilled; hence the learned complete this hymn only after knowing it (11); and whatever luck and fortune shines in women comes only by Her grace. (Continued next.)

The visible fruits are told: roaming fearless (verse 10 needs no comment, it is plain). The fault of reading without knowing such a bolt is told in 'having known': know the above bolt first, begin its removal, then read — skipping the removal, he is destroyed. And since it stands thus, the wise begin this faultless hymn only after knowing the bolt; the ruin-talk exists only to prove bolt-knowledge is a must — for casual reading too stands allowed by other sayings. 'By Her grace' means for that reason (verses 11–12, old note). (Continued in Hindi next.)
So this blessed hymn must be chanted only after unbolting it. (Verse 12, Hindi completion.) In simple words the rule is sealed: unbolt first, then chant — that order never changes.

But when this hymn is chanted softly, wealth comes rising high — all of it comes; so begin it exactly thus. (Verse 13.) In simple words: chant it and prosperity surely rises to the top — so start it in just this way.

By whose grace — lordship, luck, health, riches; killing of foes, supreme freedom — why is She not praised by people? (Verse 14, with closer.) Combined with the notes: the bolt-knowledge talk exists only to stress necessity — really, the Goddess's reading helps in every way, as other sayings prove. In simple words the sage calls out: Her grace gives power, luck, health, wealth, dead foes and topmost freedom — so why on earth do people not praise Her?

Thus ends the Lakṣmī-Kīlaka hymn. Combined with the closers: 'slowly' means unhurriedly — not in a murmur, not in the mind, for clear-voiced chanting alone is declared a must (verses 13–14, Guptavatī's seal). Pradīpa adds: 'softly' — within earshot of one's own ears — brings only some wealth; but loud chanting brings all of it, complete — so begin it loud. Then the sage, finishing the bolt-rite, calls out to people: supreme freedom is freedom-in-life itself — alas, how unlucky are these people! Leaving the wish-stone and the wish-cow — the Goddess right before their eyes — they grab a worthless cowrie-shell, that is, petty other-deity worship, for their own welfare — why? (Continued next.)

Leaving the wish-jewel and wish-cow before their eyes, why do people grab a worthless penny for their welfare — worshipping other deities instead of Her? (Verse 14, Pradīpa completion.) In simple words: the all-giving Mother stands visible, yet unlucky people chase small gods for small gains — what a pity.

Chanting this hymn softly brings small wealth; chanting loud brings all wealth — so begin it loud. (Verse 13, Hindi.) Combined with the Hindi wonder of verse 14: strange indeed — the Goddess by whose grace come power, luck, health, wealth, slain foes and supreme freedom — why is She not praised by people? Why do men not hymn the blessed Mother of the world?

Why do men not praise the blessed Mother of the world, giver of all these gifts? (Verse 14, Hindi completion.) In simple words the question hangs in the air for every reader to answer with their own voice — by chanting.

The Guru-bolt chapter stationed in the mystery-lore. Śiva said: Long ago, O stainless one, I gave this to Sanatkumāra. (Guru-kīlaka 1.) In simple words a new, deeper chapter opens — the Master-Bolt from the secret Tantras — with Śiva Himself as speaker, telling: spotless one, I first gave this to Sanatkumāra himself.

Everywhere the Caṇḍī-hymn on earth abounds; the Brahma-portion, the ritual-portion, the Tantra-portion — in every way. (Guru-kīlaka 2.) In simple words: the Caṇḍī hymn overflows everywhere on earth — through knowledge-texts, ritual-texts and Tantra-texts alike, in every path.

By this quick-fruit-giver it was blocked; then, wishing to make them fruitful on earth. (Guru-kīlaka 3.) In simple words: this fast-fruiting hymn got blocked (by the bolt) — and then, wanting to make all those paths fruitful again on earth… (the sentence completes next).

By the rite named give-and-take this mantra was bolted by Me; and what is named give-and-take — that is declared the bolt. (Guru-kīlaka 4.) In simple words Śiva names the lock openly: the give-and-take ritual with your wealth — that itself is the bolt I fixed.

From then this mantra stayed bolted by the bolt; it shall ripen to success for none — those with faces turned from the bolt. (Guru-kīlaka 5.) In simple words: since that day the mantra stays locked; bolt-ignoring chanters will not taste its fruit.

Those men who chant it with the bolt, in supreme joy — on them the Goddess is pleased; then come all prosperities. (Guru-kīlaka 6.) In simple words the key turns: chant it WITH the give-and-take rite, joyfully — and She is pleased, and every prosperity follows.

Born of You, commanded by You, Your servant, devoted to You; thinking ever of Your name — for Your cause I am appointed. (Guru-kīlaka 7.) In simple words the devotee surrenders identity itself: I am Your child, Your order, Your servant, Your lover, Your name-thinker — posted by You for Your work.

All this earned by me is Yours, O supreme Lady — kingdom, strength, treasury-house, army and every other means. (Guru-kīlaka 8.) In simple words the surrender becomes concrete: my kingdom, my strength, my treasury, my army, everything I hold — all Yours, Mother.

I shall make it Yours to use, wherever You appoint me; there, O Goddess, I ever stand, guarding only Your command. (Guru-kīlaka 9.) In simple words: use it all as You wish — post me where You will, and there I stand forever, keeping only Your order.

Having thus thought in mind, and (taken) the self-earned riches — on the dark fourteenth or eighth, composed. (Guru-kīlaka 10.) In simple words: think this surrender through, gather your honestly earned wealth, and on the dark 14th or 8th, with steady mind… (the rite follows next).

Let him offer to the great Goddess all self-earned wealth — kingdom, strength, treasury-house, and all newly earned gains. (Guru-kīlaka 11.) In simple words: lay everything honestly earned — land, power, savings, every fresh gain — at the great Goddess's feet.

'In this month, O Goddess, this is offered by me to You' — having meditated thus, then taking it back by Her grace. (Guru-kīlaka 12.) In simple words: name the month, say 'all this is Yours' — and then receive it back from Her hands as blessed grace-food.

Dividing everything fivefold — three shares for his own needs; one share he assigns for gods, ancestors and guests, for rites. (Guru-kīlaka 13, page-header dust on the verse forgiven.) In simple words the grace-wealth is split in five: three parts for himself, one part for gods-ancestors-guests and holy rites… (and one part for the teacher, next).

One share let him give to the teacher — thus the Goddess is pleased. His kingdom, strength, army and treasury flourish nobly. (Guru-kīlaka 14.) In simple words: the fifth share goes to the guru — and with the teacher honoured, She is pleased, and everything the devotee holds — land, power, army, savings — grows and grows.

Like the sea full of jewel-mines at full-moon time, glorious — having known the nine-lettered mantra, shelter of self and Absolute. (Guru-kīlaka 15.) In simple words: know the nine-lettered mantra — home of soul and God — and you swell like the full-moon sea, brimming with gems.

The essence of 'Thou art That' and such great sayings, the medicine for worldly life — the mantra called Saptashatī, all my life I chant. (Guru-kīlaka 16.) In simple words: this hymn is the cream of the great Vedānta lines, the cure for birth-and-death — 'I shall chant the Saptashatī-mantra all my life.'

Doing so, may I never meet with neglect — firm in this resolve; having begun, let him do — not doing, he is destroyed. (Guru-kīlaka 17.) In simple words: vow never to skip, not once by carelessness — begin and keep doing; starters who quit are ruined.

'May I never reject Brahman; may Brahman never reject me. May there be no rejection for me; no rejection of me.' (Guru-kīlaka 18.) In simple words the ancient prayer: never may I push God away, never may God push me away — no rejection on either side, ever.

Since the crown of the Vedas, the Chāndogya, spreads this teaching — once begun, quitting is not held good for him. (Guru-kīlaka 19.) In simple words: the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, crest-jewel of the Vedas, itself teaches this prayer — so having started, dropping it brings no good.

Never is one born in his line who knows not Brahman; never is there poverty in his line, as long as the earth stands. (Guru-kīlaka 20.) In simple words the lineage-blessing: in his family no ignorant child is ever born, and poverty never enters his home — till the earth itself lasts.

Every year let him do the autumnal and the yearly (rite); thus he gains everything, hard even for gods and demons to win. (Guru-kīlaka 21.) In simple words: keep the yearly autumn worship without fail — and win everything that even gods and demons can hardly win.

And whatever other welfare is born, moment to moment — true, true, this is true — to be guarded with effort. (Guru-kīlaka 22.) In simple words: and every other blessing that keeps arriving, instant by instant — this is true, true, true — guard this secret teaching with all your care.

To a son devoted to Brahman the great-souled father must give it; else the Goddess will surely curse him — no doubt. (Guru-kīlaka 23.) Combined with the old note: the rule in plain words — only wealth freshly earned by oneself (not father's earnings), after receiving the mantra, is offered on the dark 14th or 8th standing near the Goddess, naming place and time, resolving to please Her by give-and-take, chanting 'born of You' thrice with meaning, mentally laying 'kingdom, strength, treasury' at Her feet, taking it back as Her order, giving the fifth share to teacher or his sons, setting aside a fourth for the five daily sacrifices and duties, and using the rest freely as one likes. Lunar months count here; next month's offering covers this month's gains. That is give-and-take rite number one. Second: seekers come in three grades — low, middle, high — by how early in life blazing devotion wakes in them; but here is the exception — having taken the nine-lettered mantra and learnt its Vedānta-matching meaning from the teacher, the fit soul vows lifelong never-once-careless Saptashatī reading, and lives it. That vow never to drop the begun wisdom is rite number two. The Chāndogya lines prove it; the autumn and spring vows with ninth-day worship complete the yearly round — all within one's strength.

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: The Pradīpa voices the answer through Brahmā: O Brāhmaṇa, the holy armour of the Goddess alone — the very thing you asked for — exists; keep it like a buried treasure, and 'great sage' fits because it serves all beings.

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Brahmā said: O Brāhmaṇa, the most secret and holy means that helps all beings is the Goddess's armour itself — listen, O great sage. (Verse 2.)

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: Since the Goddess is to be meditated as nine-formed, Her nine names are given — knowing a name, you easily know whom it means. Śailaputrī: though supreme, She accepted the lowly mountain-king's daughterhood when He prayed with hard penance, out of mercy — what words for such love toward devotees, famed in the Kūrma Purāṇa! Brahmacāriṇī: Brahman is blissful reality, and carrying seekers to It is Her nature — giver of Brahmanhood. Candraghaṇṭā: the bell in Her hand, spotless like the moon; the secret lore hails Her 'the delight-giver.'

tikas.author: Pāṭhabheda-ṭippaṇī
tikas.simpleEn: Variant: some read 'and Śailaputrī'. Then word-roots: 'moon-bell' — She rings the moon, as it were, proclaiming Her own delight-giving pride; lovelier even than the moon. Kūṣmāṇḍā: the world, where bad heat — the three sufferings — lives inside the cosmic egg (the belly-like flesh-ball), She devours that world of triple pain. 'Egg' also means muscle-ball and testicle, says the dictionary.

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: The Goddess has nine faces — first Śailaputrī, second Brahmacāriṇī, third Candraghaṇṭā… (continues in the next passage).

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: Skandamātā: Skanda is Sanatkumāra, born of the Goddess's own valour — scriptures say even the wise long to be born of such a womb, so pure is She. Kātyāyanī: She appeared in sage Kātyāyana's hermitage for the gods' mission and was accepted as his daughter — ever-maiden, under no husband, fully free. Kālarātrī: the night that destroys even Time the killer of all, since at world-dissolution even Time dies. Mahāgaurī: the greatly self-respecting one — called 'dark' by Śiva in love-play, She won a fair color by penance; the Kālī Purāṇa tells it plainly.

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Fifth face Skandamātā, sixth Kātyāyanī, seventh Kālarātrī, eighth Mahāgaurī. (Verse 4.)

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: 'Giver of powers' means giver of final freedom. The nine Durgās are nine faces of the one Durgā — like a yogi's many body-forms — and those are exactly the meditation-forms the scriptures declare; I have but named them. That is also why the armour is spoken of in one number.

tikas.author: Pāṭhabheda-ṭippaṇī
tikas.simpleEn: Variant: some read 'and Siddhidātrī'.

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: The ninth face is famed as Siddhidātrī; thus the Nine Durgās are told. All these names were spoken by all-knowing Brahmā, the Veda-Lord Himself. (Verse 5.)

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: Supply while reading: 'whoever chants the nine names'. The joint sense of both verses: the one chanter plus the many others sheltered behind him — for all of them, all harm is removed.

tikas.author: Pradīpa
tikas.simpleEn: Having shown the Goddess-form to meditate in Kavaca-reading, now — lest anyone doubt the fruit — the argument from the smaller to the greater: the burning one fallen among wartime foes, once sheltered (supply this); and those terror-struck in rough, impassable, most-dangerous spots, once sheltered. (Verse 6.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: The burning one, the war-trapped one among foes, and the terror-struck in rough impassable places — all sheltered in Goddess Durgā. (Begins verses 6–7; concludes next.)

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: Having told the fruit of devotion-in-distress, now the fruit of the seeker's devotion: 'by whomsoever' — theirs is attainment. The Seven Mothers' round-the-clock work suits exactly the removal of devotees' troubles — described across two verses (8–9).

tikas.author: Pradīpa
tikas.simpleEn: Those remembered with love surely win the earlier fruit — and what to say of it, theirs is growth of duty, wealth, desire and freedom too. Now, to grow devotion, the Goddess's overflowing motherliness is shown: then the Seven Mothers in two verses (8–9).

tikas.author: Pāṭhabheda-ṭippaṇī
tikas.simpleEn: Variant: some read 'their growth'. (Running page-header dust follows, not text.) Then: to grow devotion, the Goddess's overflowing love is shown — then the Seven Mothers in two verses.

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Whoever remembers the Goddess with love surely prospers. Cāmuṇḍā sits on a corpse; Vārāhī rides a buffalo; Aindrī rides the elephant Airāvata; Vaiṣṇavī… (continues next).

tikas.author: Bhāṣya (untagged)
tikas.simpleEn: The explainers never accepted these extra verses in the Kavaca. For detail see Paṇḍit Rājakiśoramaṇi Tripathī's 'Devī-Māhātmya: A Study'.

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: Verses 10–13 (the Pradīpa notes the weapon-list about to be told).

tikas.author: Pāṭhabheda-ṭippaṇī
tikas.simpleEn: Variant: some read '…and the supreme wonderful weapon' differently. Then: the goddesses to be told are seen — and goddesses beyond the Seven Mothers, also chariot-mounted in anger for devotees' guard, are seen — by gods and men, as it were. Weapons listed (verses 10–12). Then (verse 13): the Seven Mothers hold the conch-discus-listed weapons — for what? To finish demons' bodies, to give devotees fearlessness, and to serve the gods. The feeling: even unasked, these great goddesses rush to world-guard purely from motherly love — so why should unlucky me not beg them for my own guard, like a child its mother?

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Brāhmī on Her swan, dressed in every ornament; many bejewelled, many decorated, anger-blazing goddesses seen on chariots — holding conch, discus, mace, spear, plough, club, shield, javelin, axe, noose, lance, trident and the supreme wonderful bow — to finish demons, free devotees from fear, and surely serve the gods. (Verses 10–13.)

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: From here the devotee himself starts praying, with 'O mighty' and the rest. (Verse 14.)

tikas.author: Pradīpa
tikas.simpleEn: Read this prayer-mantra first, then the Kavaca — that is the point. 'Great strength' is Her illusion-power itself; 'great eagerness' is Her zeal in world-guarding; 'destroyer of great fear' destroys death-like fear by giving wisdom. 'Hard to behold' — unseeable, as scripture says Her form stands not in sight. The 'foes' are lust, anger and kin. (Verse 14.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: O greatly strong! Greatly eager! Destroyer of great fears! (Continues next.)

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: Grammar of joining: where the goddess-name ends in the nominative, the command runs third-person; where in address, second-person — no dispute in joining. Each verb simply carries to its own line as fits.

tikas.author: Pāṭhabheda-ṭippaṇī
tikas.simpleEn: Variant: some read 'hard to behold' (in verse 14). Then the joining rule: where address-form meets third-person ('may Brāhmī guard me'), supply 'is'; and where nominative meets second-person, join the nominative word as adjective to the silent 'you'. (Verse 15.)

tikas.author: Pradīpa
tikas.simpleEn: 'In the east' — Aindrī, Indra's power, stationed east, protect me (or: protect me standing east — same, since power and holder are one; so too ahead). The fire-formed goddess is fire-power. 'May protect' carries forward. Vārāhī kills the choicest — Varāha is Yama, ancient usage — His power is Vārāhī (Yama-power, says the ten-direction-lords context; or the Vārāhī among the Seven Mothers). O Vārāhī, standing south, protect me (or: protect me standing there). Sword-bearer is Nirṛti's power. 'Protect' was split mid-verse, so supply it. (Verse 15.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: In the east may Aindrī (Indra's power) protect me; in the south-east the fire-goddess. O Vārāhī, protect me in the south; in the south-west may sword-bearer protect me. (Verse 15.)

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: Deer-rider: the wind-god rides a deer, so this is wind-power; 'protect' carries forward. Kaumārī: the ugly-prided (kutsita-mada) one is Kumāra-Kubera — His power is Kaumārī, in the direction-lords context. Kubera's guard-station comes openly ahead, yet one goddess guarding two stations is no fault. Or the Kaumārī among the Seven Mothers. Spear-holder is Īśāna's power. (Verse 16.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: In the west Vāruṇī, in the north-west the deer-riding Goddess — (continues next).

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: Brāhmī — She who fetches and revives Brahmā (all beings): O Brāhmī, standing above, protect me (or: protect my upper part — same). So below too. 'Thus' — like the ten direction-lord goddesses. Supply 'my': may Cāmuṇḍā guard my ten kin-directions — Cāmuṇḍā stationed in all ten guards me; that is the settled sense, since merely guarding empty directions serves no purpose. (Verse 17.)

tikas.author: Pāṭhabheda-ṭippaṇī
tikas.simpleEn: Variants: some read 'protect in the north' and 'in the north-east'. (Running header dust follows.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: O Brāhmī, guard me above… (continues next).

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: 'Let her stand' — may she stand firm. (Verse 18.)

tikas.author: Pradīpa
tikas.simpleEn: Jayā is a power-goddess — let her stand. Ancient usage. All for my guarding. (Verse 18.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: May Jayā stand before me, Vijayā behind, Ajitā to my left, Aparājitā to my right. (Verse 18.)

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: Join limb by limb the same way: the goddess named Udyotinī, stationed at my hair-top, guards my hair-top — and of the two patterns, whichever is unsaid in either place, supply the other there. As here in the first line stationing is supplied, in the second guarding. So everywhere. (Verse 19.)

tikas.author: Pradīpa
tikas.simpleEn: The goddess named Udyotinī, stationed at my hair-top, guards my hair-top — join every limb the same way everywhere. Umā, stationed on the crown, guards the crown — and so everywhere, supply as fits. (Verse 19.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Udyotinī in the hair-top guards it; Umā on the crown guards the crown; Mālādhārī on the forehead guards it; Yaśasvinī on the brows guards them. (Verse 19.)

tikas.author: Pāṭhabheda-ṭippaṇī
tikas.simpleEn: Variants: some read 'protect' (for 'guard'), 'throat-region' (for 'throat-middle'), and 'Śāṅkarī' (for 'Śaṅkarī').

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: Verses 20–23 (the Pradīpa notes): 'at the nostrils' means at the nose-holes (while later 'nose' alone means the nose-bridge). 'Lower' means the lower lip. (Verses 22–23.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Three-eyed one at brow-centre guards brows; death-bell at nose guards nostrils; conch-lady in both eyes guards eyes; door-keeper in both ears guards ears (20). Kālikā on cheeks, Śaṅkarī at ear-roots, Sugandhā on nose, Carcikā on upper lip guard each (21). Nectar-digit on lower lip, Sarasvatī on tongue, Kaumārī on teeth, Caṇḍikā mid-throat guard each (22). Bell-pictured goddess at throat-bell, Great Illusion at palate, love-eyed goddess at chin, all-blessing goddess on speech guard each (23).

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: 'Windpipe' means the throat-tube. (Verses 24–25.)

tikas.author: Pradīpa
tikas.simpleEn: The throat's outer part is the outer throat. Windpipe is the throat-tube. (Verse 24.) Shoulder-to-elbow is the arm; elbow-to-fingertips the hand. (Verse 25.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Bhadrakālī on the neck guards it; bow-bearer on the spine guards it; blue-throated on the outer throat guards it; Nalakūbarī in the windpipe guards it (24). Sword-bearer on both shoulders guards them; thunderbolt-bearer on both my arms guards them… (continues next).

tikas.author: Pāṭhabheda-ṭippaṇī
tikas.simpleEn: Variant: some read 'may the sword-lady guard the shoulders'. (Page number dust follows.)

tikas.author: Bhāṣya (untagged)
tikas.simpleEn: Old quoted verse: Mahābalā is declared at the shanks, Vināyakī between the knees, Nārasiṃhī at the ankles, Amitaujasī on the foot-top. (Verse 29.)

tikas.author: Bhāṣya (untagged)
tikas.simpleEn: Old quoted verse: Kauberī in the hair-pores, Vāgīśvarī on the skin — (continues: and Pārvatī in blood, marrow, fat, flesh, bone and medulla. Verse 31.)

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: Verses 26–28 need nothing. On 'at the shanks': 'declared' means famed in the lore-books and the rest — an epithet of the great-strong Goddess. (Verse 29.) 'Under the feet' is one phrase; 'under-dweller' means underworld-dweller. (Verses 30–31.)

tikas.author: Pradīpa
tikas.simpleEn: The locative reading 'in the belly' is the ancient approved one. (Verses 26–27.) 'Vindhyavāsinī the knees' is the reading. (Verse 28.) 'Declared' — famed in the lore-books and scriptures as Mahābalā, that is. (Verse 29.) 'Under the feet' is one phrase; 'under-dweller' means underworld-dweller. And though nail-guarding was already told for the spear-lady, just as one goddess guarding two stations is no fault, so two goddesses guarding one station is no fault either — hence Karālī for both toenails and teeth. (Verses 30–31.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Spear-lady on nails guards them; belly-goddess in belly guards it; Great Goddess on both breasts guards them; grief-destroyer in mind guards it (26). Lalitā in heart, spear-holder in belly, Kāminī at navel, secret-lady at secret place guard each (27). (Continues: organ, anus, waist, knees — next.)

tikas.author: Pāṭhabheda-ṭippaṇī
tikas.simpleEn: Ten variants noted honestly: Kuleśvarī (for Śūleśvarī); 'in the heart'; 'in the belly'; 'at the navel'; 'Pūtanā-Kāmikā for the organ'; 'at the anus'; 'giver of all desired boons'; 'bright ones on the foot-top'; 'may Śrī guard the toes'; 'Karālī of nails and fangs'. None adopted — all reported.

tikas.author: आगम प्रसिद्धा
tikas.simpleEn: Mahābalā on the shanks guards them; Vināyakī between the knees guards it; Nārasiṃhī on both ankles guards them; mighty Amitaujasī on the foot-top guards it (29). Śrīdharī on the toes guards them; under-feet-dweller on the soles guards them; Karālī on toenails and teeth guards them; sky-haired one on the hair guards it (30). Pore-dweller Kauberī guards the pores; speech-lady Vāgīśvarī guards the skin (31, continues).

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: The lotus is but heart-and-such; the cave is the dwelling of the breath living there — stationed in that wind, may She guard that wind, that is all. (Verse 32.)

tikas.author: Pradīpa
tikas.simpleEn: Grammar of 'entrails' aside — 'in the lotus-cave': the lotus is but heart-and-such, the cave the dwelling of the breath living there — stationed in that wind, may She guard it, say some. But since breath-guarding comes later, others take 'lotus-cave' as the heart itself, which scripture calls 'like a lotus-cave, facing down'. The goddess named Cūḍāmaṇi is famed from the blood-demon killing. (Verse 32.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Kālarātri in the entrails guards them… (continues next).

tikas.author: Pāṭhabheda-ṭippaṇī
tikas.simpleEn: Variant: some read 'O holder of righteousness'.

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: Verse 33 needs nothing. On ego and the rest: here 'mind' means the whole inner mind-stuff — and since the inner organ is fourfold with the mind, verse 26's grief-destroyer is not repeated. Or read it as 'She who destroys the mind's grief'. Apply 'breasts, may Mahādevī guard' as that very epithet joined here. The five-breaths phrase is a collective in the accusative. (Verses 34–35.)

tikas.author: Pradīpa
tikas.simpleEn: Nail-flame is the glow living in nails. The Unbreakable goddess stationed in all joints guards all joints. 'O Brāhmī, guard my vitality.' (Verse 33.) 'O follower of righteousness' — supply 'you'; 'guard' runs second-person. (Verse 34.) 'O Indrāṇī' — supply 'you are'. (Verse 35.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Flame-faced on nail-glow guards it; Unbreakable in all joints guards them; Brāhmī on vitality guards it; umbrella-lady on shadow guards it (33). Follower-of-righteousness on ego, mind, intellect and all five breaths guards them (34).

tikas.author: Pāṭhabheda-ṭippaṇī
tikas.simpleEn: Variant: some read 'wealth and learning' (for 'sons'). A longer road-verse runs in some copies — 'guard the path well, guard the road with welfare; Mahālakṣmī at the king's door, Vijayā dwelling everywhere'. (Running header dust follows.)

tikas.author: Bhāṣya (untagged)
tikas.simpleEn: Old quoted verse: if he wishes his own good, let him not take one step without the armour — always wrapped in the Kavaca, wherever he goes. (Verse 38.)

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: Verses 36–37 name the fruit of wearing. 'Not one step and the rest' means: without the worn armour — supply the rest. (Verses 38–41.)

tikas.author: Pradīpa
tikas.simpleEn: Verse 36 needs nothing. On 37: whatever station stands guard-less — why? Because left out of the armour, its mention never made — guard all that for me, O Goddess, since You are Jayantī the topmost and sin-destroyer. Then Grandfather (Brahmā) first teaches who is fit, before telling the fruit-praise: 'not one step' — if he wants his own good, let the man not go even one step bare of the armour; not a moment is to be spent without Goddess-remembrance — that is the point. As the Purāṇas say: sleeping, standing, walking the road, chatting, delighting in food — always chant the Goddess, and he is freed from bondage. So taught the rule, now He tells the fruit: wrapped, wherever he goes (verses 38–41).

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Mahālakṣmī guards sons; Bhairavī the wife; Kṣemakarī the road; all-pervading Vijayā guards in every way (36). Whatever stations the armour leaves guard-less — pious Jayantī, sin-destroyer, guard them all for me (37). Wishing his own good, let man not go one step without the armour — chanting it, he travels. Armour-wrapped, wherever he goes he gains aims and wish-fulfilling victory; whatever wished thing he thinks of, he surely gets (38–39). (Continues: supreme lordship, fearlessness — next.)

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: 'Stationary' poison means aconite and such; 'moving' means snakes and the like; 'man-made' means mutually-mixed-born — like honey and ghee in equal measure going wrong. (Verse 44.) The family-born and the rest are classes of dark deities. (Verses 45–48.)

tikas.author: Pradīpa
tikas.simpleEn: 'Divine lustre' is the lustre of pure consciousness. (Verses 42–43.) 'Black rites' are foe-made ones. (Verse 44.) The family-born and the rest are classes of dark deities; 'teaching-born' are those perfected by mere teaching — petty deity classes. 'From the king' means the honour comes from the king's side. (Verses 45–48.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Whoever reads this armour daily with rule — dawn, noon, dusk — full of faith, wins goddess-glow and stays undefeated in all three worlds (42). And more — past a hundred years, free of sudden death, all blister-pox diseases dead (43). (Continues: poisons, rites, spirit-hosts — next.)

tikas.author: अफीम, धतूरे आदि का
tikas.simpleEn: Then every poison — plant (aconite and the like), moving (snake, scorpion and the like), and man-made (like opium blended with oils) — every spell, diagram and black rite on earth; crawlers, flyers, water-born, teaching-born, inborn, clan troops, garland-Ḍākinīs, Śākinīs, sky-terrors, mighty Ḍākinīs, planets, ghosts, goblins, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, demons, brahmin-ghosts, vampires, Kuṣmāṇḍas, Bhairavas — all perish merely at the sight of the armour-hearted man; and that best of men rises in royal honour, blazes with supreme glow, and grows in fame that garlands the earth (44–48).

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: On 'let him chant': here 'having first done the armour, let him chant the Saptashatī' is the rule — and 'having done' only repeats what the armour's limbship of the Caṇḍī-reading already proves (by the armour's very name and by other sayings, the armour's being a limb of Caṇḍī-reading stands proved). The earlier telling of other side-fruits is no fault, by the side-desire rule accepting a separate outer use. 'As long as the earth-disc' and the rest is praise-speech like full-perfection fruit-speech. 'First' ordains mere firstness in time — and since no gaplessness is told here, the night-hymn wrap-around stands explained elsewhere ('read the night-hymn first'); by beginning-middle-end words and the step-word the Vedic order stands unbreakable, so the nine-lettered sits before the night-hymn itself. So too the Argala's 'having read this hymn, let man read the great hymn' teaches only limb-and-whole kinship — as with 'having eaten today, he goes tomorrow', the -having-done form works even with a gap, so the Vedic order stands unharmed and the kinship holds despite gaps. But Kavaca and Argala, by reading alone, teach the order — like the ten-callers' calls and chants, by the drawing-together order-rule the order is fixed: Kavaca, Argala, nine-lettered, night-hymn, Caṇḍī-praise; and after counting praise-and-chant, Goddess-hymn, nine-lettered and mysteries follow in order. (Verses 49–51. Thus ends the Guptavatī explanation of the Goddess-armour.)

tikas.author: Pradīpa
tikas.simpleEn: Now the armour's being a limb of the Saptashatī is ordained. 'Let him chant': first of all. 'Holds' — the endless serpent holds and bears the earth-disc, that long. (Verse 49.) The supreme station he wins through wisdom — always, by rule. Mahāmāyā is Brahman veiled by the all-cause illusion — by Her grace. As scripture says: 'whom the Self chooses, by him It is won; the Self opens Its own body to him' — and 'who knows this power of illusion conquers death, crosses sin, and reaches deathlessness' — and 'I Myself speak this, tasted by gods and men' — and 'Pārvatī is supreme wisdom, giver of Brahman-wisdom.' Specially for beings — no ground for doubt here, says the Sūta Saṃhitā. (Verses 50–51.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Whoever first reads the armour and then reads the Saptashatī or Caṇḍī — his line of sons and grandsons stays on earth as long as the earth-disc holds mountains, forests and woods. And after the body's end, by holy Mahāmāyā's grace he surely reaches that eternal supreme station, hard even for gods. (Verses 49–51, Hindi.) One book adds 'he gains the supreme form and rejoices with Śiva' — but since most books don't agree, it stays out of the original. Then the Argala hymn begins: its seer is Viṣṇu, metre anuṣṭup, deity great Lakṣmī, purpose — pleasing Mother Jagadambā as a limb of the Saptashatī chant; and Mārkaṇḍeya speaks.

tikas.author: Guptavatī
tikas.simpleEn: 'Victorious one': 'blessed one' takes the possessing sense. (Verse 1.)

tikas.author: Pradīpa
tikas.simpleEn: Now the Argala explanation begins. First, the aimed Goddess's qualities, fit for meditation: 'Victorious one' — the topmost victor, since the Mother as Brahman veiled by the three balanced qualities causes all. 'Blessed one': She takes away devotees' creeping through birth-and-death and grants freedom — 'his breaths do not depart' says scripture. 'Dark one': She swallows all this at world-end — 'Brahman and warriorhood both become His food, with Death as sauce' says scripture. 'Kind-dark one': She takes goodness and joy to give devotees — 'kind-dark, joy-giver' as the secret lore phrases it. 'Skull-holder': skull means head-bone (says the dictionary) — having killed Brahmā and the rest, holding their skulls, She roams at world-end; or lotus-universe in hand; the secret lore hails Her 'lotus-universe-handed supreme skull-bearer'. 'Hard-to-reach': reached with pain through yoga, ritual and worship — 'that Durgā, hard to reach' says the Atharvaśiras. 'Forbearing': She bears all faults of devotees and others, being Mother, overflowing with mercy. 'Goodness': Herself pure consciousness — as the Sūta Saṃhitā sings at length: the changeless, ever-blissful awareness, destroyer of worldliness, supreme Goddess, one with Śiva, maker of good. 'Nourisher': holder of the whole expanse — 'I move with Rudras and Vasus, I bear Mitra-Varuṇa, Indra-Agni and the Aśvins' says scripture. 'Svāhā feeds the gods, Svadhā feeds the ancestors.' O possessor of all these great qualities — to You, salutation alone; for serving such a One in full, who has the strength? That is the feeling. (Verse 1.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
tikas.simpleEn: Mārkaṇḍeya the seer, teaching his students the Goddess's praise, said — Jayantī 1, Maṅgalā 2… (continues).

tikas.author: Pradīpa
tikas.simpleEn: 'What did He say? All this' — of all mantras, the un-bolter in the coming manner: since it destroys the curse-form bolt blocking all mantra success, the Saptashatī hymn is the un-bolter by pointer-sense — know it all, worship it, is the sense. And if you ask whether other mantra practices bring no safety, that this alone is grasped — it does bring, says 'he too'. The man constantly busy in the work of chanting many mantras, endlessly devoted — that devoted man too attains all welfare, all weal. (Verse 2.)

tikas.author: Candraprabhā
